Fix brass/copper pyramid strips along the bottom face of the beam. 4. Physically move the bedstead entirely clear of the beam's vertical shadow.

rules_matrix.rule_description: No mirror, dressing table mirror, mirrored wardrobe panel, or reflective TV screen must directly reflect the reclining body or the bedstead while asleep.

rules_matrix.remedial_measures: 1. Relocate all mirrors to the North or East interior walls where they reflect positive cosmic energy without capturing the bed. 2. If wardrobe mirrors cannot be removed, cover them completely with an opaque, non-sheer cloth or drape every night before sleeping. 3. Never install mirrored ceiling panels above the bed.

rules_matrix.remedial_measures: 1. Reposition the bed diagonally or offset from the door swing path. 2. Place a solid wooden screen, chest of drawers, or thick curtain between the door opening and the bed to buffer rushing airflow.

interpretation: Bedroom Vastu in classical Sanskrit treatises represents an exquisite convergence of bio-geomagnetism, environmental psychology, circadian neurobiology, and structural architecture. The human head functions as the positive magnetic pole of the physical body. Aligning the head towards the South establishes an attractive magnetic circuit with the Earth's geomagnetic South, which stabilizes arterial blood pressure, reduces cardiac workload during sleep, and allows uninterrupted delta-wave brain states essential for cellular repair and immune regeneration. Conversely, pointing the head towards the North sets up a violent repulsive magnetic dynamic that causes micro-vascular tension in cerebral blood vessels, elevated cortisol, chronic insomnia, and psychological agitation. In terms of spatial zoning, the South-West (Nairṛtya) is ruled by the Earth element (Pṛthvī) and the ancestral Pitṛs, signifying maximum mass, thermal inertia, and immobility. Anchoring the master bedroom in the South-West provides the head of the family with foundational leadership authority, emotional equilibrium, and economic stability. Rooms for youth, guests, and daughters are strategically mapped to dynamic zones: the North-West (governed by Vāyu / Air) facilitates mobility, cordial temporary stays for visitors, and timely matrimonial transition for daughters without creating stagnation. Architectural elements such as overhead beams (Tulā-doṣa) and reflective mirrors (Darpaṇa-vedha) are rigorously regulated to shield the sleeper's vulnerable astral and biological field from gravitational shear stress and reflective energetic exhaustion.
variation_note: Textual and regional traditions exhibit distinct specialized nuances while upholding core axioms. In the South Indian Dravidian tradition (Mayamata and Mānasāra), great emphasis is placed on multi-storey royal suites, structural heaviness, and botanical timber selection (Śayyā-lakṣaṇa), where specific sacred hard woods (such as Śāla, Asana, and Khadira) are mandated for the bedstead to harmonize with planetary vibrations. In the Kerala vernacular tradition (Manuṣyālaya Candrikā), the master suite is anchored in the Kanni-mūla (South-West corner) of the timber Nālukettu courtyard system; it mandates strict adherence to the avoidance of Tulā-doṣa (overhead structural tie-beams) and prohibits bedrooms in the Vaṭakkini (Northern block) for elders. In the Western and Central Indian classical traditions (Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra of King Bhoja and Viśvakarma Prakāśa), room allocations are tightly linked to the 81-pada Paramaśāyika grid, detailing planetary rulerships and warning against the severe ascetic and financial ruin caused by master bedchambers in the North-East (Īśāna). In modern high-rise apartments where homeowners cannot alter structural concrete columns or exterior walls, classical Vastu applies micro-zoning (allocating the master bed to the SW sector of the apartment, and the bed to the SW sub-quadrant of that room), utilizing false ceilings to encase concrete beams and wooden screening partitions to neutralize door-piercing (Dvāra-vedha).

In modern combined bathrooms, the wet bathing area should occupy the North-East or East sector of the room, segregated from the commode by a glass partition or curtain.

interpretation: Toilet and bathroom design in classical Vāstu Shastra represents one of the world's earliest systematic codes of preventive epidemiology, environmental sanitation, and bio-energetic zoning. Classical Sanskrit treatises make a fundamental ontological distinction between Snāna (sacred purification through clean, living water) and Śauca (the sanitary voiding of human metabolic waste). Pure water bathing belongs to the solar East and North-East, where early ultraviolet rays sterilize the damp atmosphere and stimulate human endocrine vitality. Conversely, human waste disposal (Utṣarga-sthāna) is strictly relegated to zones designed for detoxification and dispersal: West-North-West (WNW, ruled by Asura and Śoṣa, the deities of biological release and drying), South-South-West (SSW, the zone of metabolic excretion and expenditure), and North-West (Vāyavya, where the kinetic wind element rapidly dilutes and sweeps away foul ammoniacal gases and methane). Classical texts pronounce severe prohibitions against locating toilets in the North-East (Īśāna, the cosmic crown and spiritual receptor), the South-West (Nairṛtya, the earth foundation and marital anchor), and the Brahmasthāna (the cosmic navel and heart). Polluting these sensitive nodes with human excreta causes severe systemic pathologies: neurological disorders, financial ruin, relationship breakdown, and chronic morbidity. The mandatory alignment for the commode user—facing North or South—harmonizes the human colon with the Earth's geomagnetic meridians, assisting natural peristalsis while strictly honoring the sacred solar trajectory.
variation_note: Traditional and regional architectural practices reveal fascinating evolutionary adaptations across India's geographical zones. In the traditional Kerala timber architecture documented in Manuṣyālaya Candrikā and Tantrasamuccaya, toilets were never permitted inside the main residential wooden dwelling (Nālukettu or Ettukettu). Instead, they were constructed as completely detached outdoor privies (Kākṣi-veśma) in the outer Vāyavya (North-West) compound, safely separated from the central Ayana and positioned downstream from the sacred domestic well (Kiṇaru) situated in the North-East. In the arid and rocky terrains of Western India and the Deccan palaces documented in Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra and Aparājitapṛcchā, elaborate gravity-assisted stone conduits (Praṇāla) and ventilated turrets were engineered on outer ramparts in the North-West, discharging waste into deep exterior subterranean soakways (Gartas) away from internal aquifers. In contemporary 21st-century multi-storey apartments where bathrooms are embedded inside bedrooms and plumbing stacks are structurally fixed by civil engineers, classical Vastu adapts through micro-zoning: sub-dividing the master bedroom suite into 16 micro-zones to place the commode in the micro-WNW or micro-NW, using non-invasive elemental boundary remedies (copper, brass, lead, or aluminium floor strips), maintaining pneumatic door closures, and physically decoupling wet bathing zones from dry water closets.
